  PROBLEM: The check "$(" in word parses a word holding $( as a command line of its own, but the lexer strips quotes, so a single-quoted literal $( (which is not a command substitution) is treated as one.   WHY: Over-masking alters the reported command text, showing a masked credential where none existed. No credential leaks, but the false positive changes the command display. The plan G1 explicitly accepts over-masking as safe and documents it in the changelog.

- workflow-templates/.claude/scripts/permission_prompts.py, `_segment_credentials()` at lines 608-610, the `if "$(" in word:` check | severity=low | confidence=3
  PROBLEM: The code parses any word containing `$(` as a command line, but cannot distinguish between `$(` inside double quotes (actual command substitution) vs single quotes (literal text). After the lexer strips quotes, `'$(mysql -pS3cretPass)'` and `"$(mysql -pS3cretPass)"` both produce the same token, so literal text in single quotes is treated as executable code.
  WHY: For `echo '$(mysql -pS3cretPass)'`, the code extracts `S3cretPass` as a credential and masks it, even though it's literal text. This is over-masking (false positive), not under-masking, so no credential leaks. The code's design principle (documented in the progress log lessons) is "over-masking is safe, a wrong single guess leaks." While safe, this case is undocumented and untested.
